description: We are DoStar, a student team interested in robotics, technology, and problem-solving. We have experience building robots and working on projects involving software, AI, and engineering. We have also taken part in local and international competitions. For NASA Space Apps, we want to learn, work with NASA data, and build a useful project together. We welcome teammates interested in coding, data analysis, design, science, or research.
summary:
One wildfire can show up as a single hotspot in MODIS data and several in VIIRS data. That makes it hard to tell whether a season had more fire activity or the satellites simply picked up more detail.
We built Kyzyl Aspan, an interactive Burning Activity Calendar that lets users pick an area and compare fire activity across seasons. The app filters low-confidence detections and recurring heat sources such as gas flares, then puts observations from both instruments on the same hexagonal grid. A cell counts once per day for each instrument, even if it contains several hotspots. We use the years when both instruments were collecting data to adjust for the remaining difference and show uncertainty alongside the estimates.
The public prototype uses synthetic data modeled on NASA FIRMS records. It also includes simulations of onboard hotspot screening and satellite downlink planning. The calendar is designed to help land managers and researchers see when fire activity usually peaks and spot unusual periods worth a closer look.
details:
We built Kyzyl Aspan, a web app that turns MODIS and VIIRS hotspot records into a calendar of fire activity. A user can pick an area on the map, compare seasons, and see which months usually have the most activity. The app also flags periods that stand out from the local record.
The challenge is that the two instruments see the ground at different resolutions. A fire front might appear as one MODIS hotspot and several VIIRS hotspots. We filter low-confidence detections and use recurring signals to identify persistent heat sources such as gas flares. Then we put the remaining points on a shared H3 hexagonal grid. For each instrument, a cell counts once per day if it contains at least one detection. In our synthetic Kazakhstan demo, this brought the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio from 3.90 for raw hotspots to 2.04 for active cells per day. We use the years when both instruments observed the same region to adjust for the remaining gap and show an uncertainty interval alongside the results.
We built the prototype in TypeScript, used H3 for spatial indexing, and deployed it on Vercel. When a user requests a regional briefing, Gemini receives the calculated statistics and explains them in plain language. The app can produce a summary using preset rules when Gemini is unavailable. The public demo runs on synthetic data structured like NASA FIRMS records.
We also built two browser simulations to explore what happens before a hotspot reaches the calendar. KOZ screens a simulated thermal scene and prepares a 16-byte alert for a candidate that needs urgent attention. SAULE compares possible downlink windows using orbit geometry, ground station visibility, and weather.
We considered how sensor resolution, overpass timing, and cloud cover can change which hotspots appear in the record. For a land manager, the calendar could help identify when to schedule extra monitoring. For a researcher, it offers a way to spot an unusual season and inspect the observations behind it.
